targets.from: judgement values from the drafter's reading of the sources and knowledge of the species (2026-11-04), no photographs measured; to be replaced by photo measurements: a few thick, leaning, sparsely branched spiny canes, bare below, each crowned by a tier of huge flat leaves held horizontally like umbrellas

young.note: a single cane with a few leaves at the top, by a seep

old.note: a sprawling colony of canes bent over and rooting along a wet bench, their leaves a continuous umbrella at head height

description: A fearsome shrub of the wettest ground, 1-3 m, whose thick canes bristle with yellow spines and lean and sprawl along seeps and streambanks. At the top of each cane spread enormous maple-like leaves, spiny on the veins, held flat to catch the forest's dim light, with a spike of scarlet berries above them in late summer.

season_notes.winter: Bare, crooked spiny canes, the berries gone.
season_notes.spring: Leaves open late, in May, unfolding to 20-40 cm across.
season_notes.summer: Upright pyramids of greenish-white flowers become a head of shiny scarlet berries by August.
season_notes.fall: Leaves turn yellow and drop early, in September-October.

riparian.water: A wet-site indicator: shaded springs, seeps, streamsides and wet bottoms where water moves through the soil (FEIS).

range.where: seeps and streambanks of the Olympic lowland and lower slopes, from the rain forest valleys into the silver fir zone; Alaska to Oregon and inland to Montana, with outliers around Lake Superior

notes: Grown from blue elderberry (the library's broad-leaved multi-stem shrub with big leaves and berry heads) as a 'shrub' of few, leaning canes with leaves only near their tops (crown base 0.45, an inverse cone) and huge palmately lobed leaves (lobed_large, 7 lobes, 30 cm) in place of the elder's pinnate ones. The canes' dense yellow spines and the spines on the leaf veins are not drawn; the bark colour is a pale brown-yellow for them. Its real architecture, an unbranched or little-branched cane topped by a rosette of leaves (Corner's model), is closer than the template's branching suggests; the template's level counts may need lowering after a look in the lineup. The scarlet berry head stands above the leaves; the 'candle' flower form stands in for its upright, pyramidal panicle. FEIS: deer and elk use it only lightly (Roosevelt elk about 3% of the summer diet on the Pacific coast), being prickly; bears eat the berries, and the seeds, leaves and stems. Only the bear and deer are in the animal library.
